1.pericope_label: Make a joyful noise unto God, all ye lands... He ruleth by his power for ever; his eyes behold the nations

schools.summary: Ellicott works on the wording — 'better, sing aloud, or shout', 'literally, play on the harp' — and suspects the text's arrangement at the third verse, repairing it as 'ascribe glory (and) speak praise to God'; he makes the watching eyes military and corrects the flood. Delitzsch works from position instead, placing the psalm in a series linked by shared watchwords and noting that of the fifty-five psalms headed 'to the chief musician', this and its neighbour alone are anonymous.

Calvin admits the dating is beyond recovery — 'we have nothing but conjecture to offer' — and prefers the return from Babylon over Hezekiah's deliverance. Gill escapes the problem by referring the whole psalm forward to the Messiah and the latter day.

Clarke finds no author in any version but the Arabic, denies the ancient title 'psalm of the resurrection', and reads the Babylonian return throughout; he presses 'thine enemies submit' to its literal 'lie unto thee', and claims the promised end of idolatry as historically fulfilled. Wesley claims the ancestral memory for the living.

Spurgeon distinguishes the silent song of Zion from the joyful noise of the popular assembly, while warning that 'we need not so much noise, as joyful noise'; Henry unfolds the summons into God's glory, man's duty, a prediction of Gentile conversion, and the poet's own good-will, and insists praise be 'open and public'.

Augustine defines jubilation as sound without words — 'the pleasure of a thing imagined which cannot be expressed' — and turns the psalm's 'all lands' against the divided: 'whosoever holdeth a part and from the whole is cut off, should howl, not jubilate.'

debates.question: What occasion does the psalm belong to?

positions.view: Undeterminable, but most probably the opening of the temple after the return from Babylon.
The Babylonian return, read through the whole psalm — the singers being those 'now on return to your own land'.
Neither: the psalm looks forward to the Messiah and the latter day.

debates.question: Is the rejoicing at the sea past or wished for?

positions.view: Past. The future rendering is 'unnatural'; the cohortative may refer to the past where the writer 'throws himself back'.
Optative. 'The verb is properly optative — there... let us rejoice', which 'is more in keeping with the first verses of the psalm'.

outliers.view: The only voice to read the universal summons polemically, as an argument against schism rather than an invitation to the nations.

themes: Make a joyful noise unto God, all ye lands:
Sing forth the honour of his name: make his praise glorious.
Say unto God, How terrible art thou in thy works! through the greatness of thy power shall thine enemies submit themselves unto thee.
All the earth shall worship thee, and shall sing unto thee; they shall sing to thy name. Selah.
Come and see the works of God: he is terrible in his doing toward the children of men.
He turned the sea into dry land: they went through the flood on foot: there did we rejoice in him.
He ruleth by his power for ever; his eyes behold the nations: let not the rebellious exalt themselves. Selah.

8.pericope_label: O bless our God, ye people... we went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place

schools.summary: Ellicott reads 'holdeth our soul in life' as simple preservation, 'as the parallelism shows', and reports the contest over the net: the word means net elsewhere, but 'stronghold' is 'more in keeping with the other images of violence and oppression', the whole stanza raising 'a picture of the direst tyranny'. Delitzsch keeps the smelting-furnace as a figure of purifying suffering.

Gill denies the natural reading of the ninth verse outright — it is 'not to be understood of... the preservation of natural life, which is common to all men' — and takes the proving to have found the grace genuine, 'not reprobate silver'.

Clarke supplies the concrete sense throughout: the preservation covers 'our life, our liberty, and our religion'; the trying is refiner's work where the metal itself is in doubt; the net is Pharaoh's word that the wilderness had shut them in; the riding is cavalry among broken infantry; and the wealthy place is 'a well watered place, to wit, the land of Judea'.

Henry makes the held soul precarious — 'apt to slip through our fingers' — and providence 'a continued creation', raising the standard to 'not existence, but happiness'. Spurgeon takes the unmoved feet as the greater mercy, Satan being unable even to trip the saints up.

debates.question: What is it to be held in life?

positions.view: Natural preservation — being kept alive, and kept from falling.
Not that at all, which 'is common to all men', but eternal life ordained and procured, and a principle of spiritual life preserved.

debates.question: Is it a net or a stronghold they were brought into?

positions.view: A net — the word's ordinary sense here, and the versions', with the entangled Israelites at the sea for illustration.
Probably a stronghold, which 'is more in keeping with the other images of violence and oppression'.

debates.question: Where were they brought out to?

positions.view: A wealthy place read geographically: 'a well watered place, to wit, the land of Judea'.
'To refreshment', with the ancient versions, 'certainly more in keeping with the figures employed' — or, with a slight change, 'a broad place'.

outliers.view: The only voice to reject the natural sense of preservation in life as beneath the verse, since it belongs to all men alike.

themes: O bless our God, ye people, and make the voice of his praise to be heard:
Which holdeth our soul in life, and suffereth not our feet to be moved.
For thou, O God, hast proved us: thou hast tried us, as silver is tried.
Thou broughtest us into the net; thou laidst affliction upon our loins.
Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place.

13.pericope_label: I will go into thy house with burnt offerings: I will pay thee my vows... I will offer bullocks with goats

schools.summary: Ellicott argues from the scale and the ritual that the singular cannot be an individual — 'such a holocaust could hardly have been vowed by a single person. It is the community that speaks' — and reads the incense as the ascending smoke of the sacrifice. Delitzsch splits the difference, the poet speaking for himself but as a member of the community.
Gill agrees on the grade of the victims, 'of the fattest of the flock; that is, of the best', and takes the uttered vow as public and irrevocable, 'from which there is no going back'.

Clarke fixes the passage to the return and the vows to exile, quotes an old psalter's confession that 'I am noght, and thou arte all', and observes how distress produces vows that prosperity forgets; Wesley reduces the speaker to a representative, 'one speaks in the name of all the rest'.

Spurgeon insists the singular is real, since 'the best public form must fail to meet each individual case', and presses the discharging of vows; Henry reads the offerings as deliberate expense, since 'God, who is the best, must be served with the best we have', and finds Christ's intercession typified in the incense.

debates.question: Is the 'I' of these verses an individual or the community?

positions.view: The community. The holocaust is too large for one man, and the ram was enjoined for the high priest, a tribal head, or a Nazarite — not for an individual.
A real individual, whose sense of personal indebtedness makes him 'utter a song of his own' alongside the common thanksgiving.
Both: the poet speaks for himself, but 'as the diversity and the kind of the sacrifices show, as being a member of the community at large'.

debates.question: What were the lips said to have done?

positions.view: Opened — the verb's root sense, making the vow public and binding.
Something less deliberate: the words were 'blurted out, as we say in common speech'.

outliers.view: The only voice to turn the verse into a caution about vows themselves, noting how often resolutions formed in calamity 'are forgotten when affliction and calamity are removed'.

themes: I will go into thy house with burnt offerings: I will pay thee my vows,
Which my lips have uttered, and my mouth hath spoken, when I was in trouble.
I will offer unto thee burnt sacrifices of fatlings, with the incense of rams; I will offer bullocks with goats. Selah.

16.pericope_label: Come and hear, all ye that fear God, and I will declare what he hath done for my soul... Blessed be God, which hath not turned away my prayer

schools.summary: Ellicott catches the idiom of praise 'under my tongue', 'akin to our on the tip of the tongue'; sharpens the condition to a past hypothetical — 'if I had seen evil... the Lord would not have heard me' — and alone draws a dating conclusion from it, that a protestation of innocence made for the community 'marks a late period for the composition'. Delitzsch takes the address at its widest and the crying as audible.

Gill distinguishes the regard forbidden from the regard required: there is iniquity in every good man's heart, to be watched and loathed but not 'nourished and cherished'; and he runs the argument backwards, the answered prayer proving the heart was not false.

Clarke locates the fault in pretence — professing sorrow while loving the sin — and closes by pointing back to the audience: 'thus he told them what God had done for his soul.' Wesley confines it to the interior: 'if my heart had been false to God, although I might have forborne outward acts.'
Spurgeon builds on the change of verb from seeing to hearing, restricts the audience to the God-fearing, and demands first-hand testimony, since 'second-hand experience is like cauld kale het again'.

debates.question: How wide is the summons to hear?

positions.view: Restricted. Inward soul matters need selected hearers; the profane would only find material for comedy.
Unrestricted in extent: addressed 'to all who fear God, wheresoever such are to be found on the face of the earth'.

debates.question: What does regarding iniquity in the heart mean?

positions.view: Looking on it 'with approbation' — as against the regard that guards against it and loathes it, which every good man owes his own heart.
Having it 'purposely in view' — either forming wicked schemes or viewing wickedness in others complacently. 'One may not be pardoned and retain the offence.'
Pretending — professing repentance while loving the sin, or being false at heart while the outward acts are forborne.

outliers.view: The only voice to make the protestation of innocence evidence for the psalm's date, taking a corporate claim of clean hands as a mark of late composition.

themes: Come and hear, all ye that fear God, and I will declare what he hath done for my soul.
I cried unto him with my mouth, and he was extolled with my tongue.
If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me:
But verily God hath heard me; he hath attended to the voice of my prayer.
Blessed be God, which hath not turned away my prayer, nor his mercy from me.
